questions.question_text: Object R raises water by $54$ mL. Object S raises it by $69$ mL. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: S has $15\text{ cm}^3$ more volume than R.
R has $15\text{ cm}^3$ more volume than S.
options.why: Reverses which object caused the larger rise.

options.text: S has $123\text{ cm}^3$ more volume than R.
options.why: Adds the two rises instead of finding their difference.

questions.solution_text: $69-54=15$, and S caused the larger rise.

questions.question_text: Two objects each change a water level by $37$ mL. What can be concluded?

options.why: Confuses volume measured by displacement with mass.

options.text: They must be the same shape.
options.why: Assumes equal volume forces equal shape.
Invents an ordering despite equal rises.

questions.solution_text: Equal water-level rises mean equal displaced volumes.

questions.question_text: Why does a floating object need to be pushed fully below the water for this method?

options.text: Only the submerged part displaces water.
Water measures mass only at the bottom.
options.why: Confuses displacement volume with a mass measurement.

options.text: The container scale works only when covered.
options.why: Invents a condition unrelated to the measuring scale.
Incorrectly treats floating as absence of occupied space.

questions.solution_text: Full submersion makes the displaced water equal the whole object’s volume.

questions.question_text: A student calculates $480-545=-65$ mL for a submerged object. What correction is needed?

options.why: Adds the readings instead of finding the rise.
Accepts an impossible negative volume caused by reversed subtraction.
Treats the incorrect difference as another water reading.

questions.solution_text: The rise is after minus before, so $545-480=65$ mL.
